2.1 1) Types of Missingness
In order to understand the specific types of missingness, we must first define some key terms.
\[ \text{Complete Data: } \text{Y = } (\text{Y}_{ij})\] \[ \text{Missing Data Indicator: } \text{M = } (\text{M}_{ij})\]
For a specific scenario or dataset, we can think of Y, or the complete data set for that scenario as
\[\text{Y}_i = f(Y \mid \theta)\]
Where Y represents the complete dataset for the complete population, and theta contains all the parameters for that specific population.
From these definitions, we can describe the missing data mechanism as the probability of the exact type missingness, conditioned on our observed dataset, giving us this equation:
\[f(M \mid Y, \phi)\]
In this equation phi represents the - the paramters of what
a) Missing Completely at Random - MCAR
\[f(M \mid Y, \phi) = f(M \mid \phi)\]
In this case, M is independent of Y, but may or may not independent of phi(this is unknown). In this case, phi represents the unknown paramters, or the population parameters we’re trying to estimate given we had complete data. - could include a missingness paramter within phi
